claims.text: An adaptive enhanced-sampling protocol can directly compute free-energy differences between solid and liquid high-entropy-alloy phases.
Such free-energy calculations enable accurate determination of melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The approach is applicable across a broad range of multi-principal-element compositions in the high-entropy-alloy family.
Umbrella sampling, metadynamics, or advanced thermodynamic integration can be combined with dynamic selection of melting-sensitive order parameters for HEAs.
The proposed adaptive order parameter captures critical changes in local atomic arrangements and long-range order during melting.
The intersection of solid and liquid free-energy curves defines the melting temperature.
Phase stability is governed by Gibbs free energy, with the stable phase having the lowest Gibbs free energy.
The enthalpy and entropy of fusion can be obtained directly from solid-liquid free-energy differences.
Monitoring simulated volume during the solid-liquid transition yields the volume change at melting.
Liquid-phase thermodynamic properties can be extracted from the free-energy profile in the liquid regime.
The protocol will predict HEA melting temperatures with approximately 5–10% error relative to high-resolution experiments.
Fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting-volume changes will be quantitatively accurate and reproduce systematic compositional trends across HEAs.
Traditional calorimetry and standard first-principles or Monte Carlo methods are limited by HEA compositional complexity or high computational cost.
The method is predominantly applicable near the melting temperature under controlled pressure.
Extremely sluggish atomic dynamics or inadequate order parameters can reduce the effectiveness of the method.
Unforeseen short-range ordering can place alloy behavior outside the method's resolution.
Quantitative performance depends on order-parameter fidelity, sampling efficiency, extreme compositions, and kinetic barriers.
Deviation of computed melting temperature and fusion enthalpy by more than 15% from experiment would falsify the approach.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the melting point is where the solid and liquid Gibbs free energies intersect, so their free-energy difference is zero there, but it also says fusion enthalpy is obtained from the free-energy difference at that same temperature. A nonzero fusion enthalpy generally requires enthalpy evaluation or temperature derivatives of the free-energy difference, not the zero coexistence free-energy difference itself.
